hints: Look closely at where the oxygen bridge joins the two rings. One side joins at carbon 1, but the other side joins to a CH2 group, not directly to the ring.

Recall the difference between 1,4 glycosidic links that make straight chains and 1,6 glycosidic links that make branch points, and check which listed molecules are polysaccharides and which is a protein.
walkthrough:
**Identify the monomers**

Both rings are six-sided with a CH2OH or CH2 group. That tells you they are hexose sugars, glucose monomers. So the bond between them must be a glycosidic bond, not a peptide bond.

**Spot the special 1 to 6 link**

The oxygen in the middle connects carbon 1 of the upper glucose to carbon 6 (the CH2 outside the ring) of the lower glucose. This is a 1,6-glycosidic bond. It sticks out sideways and creates a branch point.

**Match to branched polysaccharides**

Straight chains use 1,4-glycosidic bonds, but branches need 1,6-glycosidic bonds. Amylopectin and glycogen are both highly branched, and starch contains amylopectin, so all three contain this bond. Amylase is an enzyme made of amino acids, so it uses peptide bonds, not glycosidic bonds.

options.A: Incorrect because amylase is a protein enzyme, so it contains peptide bonds between amino acids, not glycosidic bonds between glucoses.
options.B: Incorrect because it includes amylase (a protein) and it leaves out starch, which does contain this branch bond in its amylopectin component.
options.C: Correct because amylopectin, glycogen and starch (which contains amylopectin) are all branched glucose polysaccharides held together with 1,6-glycosidic branch bonds.
options.D: Incorrect because it includes amylase, which has no glycosidic bonds, and it leaves out amylopectin, which is a classic example of a branched molecule with 1,6 links.
